source_text:
Cum igitur aut fortuna caeca aut incerta natura sit, quanto uenerabilius ac melius antistitem ueritatis maiorum excipere disciplinam, religiones traditas colere, deos, quos a parentibus ante inbutus es timere quam nosse familiarius, adorare, nec de numinibus ferre sententiam, sed prioribus credere, qui adhuc rudi saeculo in ipsis mundi natalibus meruerunt deos uel faciles habere uel reges? inde adeo per uniuersa imperia, prouincias, oppida uidemus singulos sacrorum ritus gentiles habere et deos colere municipes, ut Eleusinios Cererem, Phrygas Matrem, Epidaurios Aesculapium, Chaldaeos Belum, Astarten Syros, Dianam Taurios, Gallos Mercurium, numina uniuersa Romanos.
sic eorum potestas et auctoritas totius orbis ambitum occupauit, sic imperium suum ultra solis uias et ipsius Oceani limites propagauit, dum exercent in armis uirtutem religiosam, dum urbem muniunt sacrorum religionibus, castis uirginibus, multis honoribus ac nominibus sacerdotum, dum obsessi et citra solum Capitolium capti colunt deos, quos alius iam spreuisset iratos, et per Gallorum acies mirantium superstitionis audaciam pergunt telis inermes, sed cultu religionis armati, dum captis hostilibus moenibus adhuc ferociente uictoria numina uicta uenerantur, dum undique hospites deos quaerunt et suos faciunt, dum aras extruunt interdum etiam ignotis numinibus et manibus.
sic dum uniuersarum gentium sacra suscipiunt, etiam regna meruerunt. hinc perpetuus uenerationis tenor mansit, quae longa aetate non infringitur, sed augetur: quippe antiquitas caerimoniis atque fanis tantum sanctitatis tribuere consueuit quantum adstruxerit uetustatis.
orientation: Caecilius is still speaking, arguing that since fortune or nature is blind, it is better to follow the traditional worship of the gods handed down by ancestors.
pass_a_gloss: Since therefore either blind fortune or uncertain nature is, how much more venerable and better to receive the teaching of ancestors as the priest of truth, to cultivate the religions handed down, to adore the gods, whom you were steeped in by parents before to fear than to know more intimately, and not to bring forth an opinion about the deities, but to believe the earlier men, who in a still rude age in the very birth of the world merited to have the gods either favorable or as kings? Thence indeed through all empires, provinces, towns we see individual peoples having their own rites of sacred things and cultivating municipal gods, so that the Eleusinians cultivate Ceres, the Phrygians the Mother, the Epidaurians Aesculapius, the Chaldaeans Belus, the Syrians Astarte, the Taurians Diana, the Gauls Mercury, the Romans all the deities. Thus their power and authority occupied the circuit of the whole world, thus they extended their empire beyond the paths of the sun and the limits of Ocean itself, while they exercise religious virtue in arms, while they fortify the city with the religions of sacred rites, with chaste virgins, with many honors and names of priests, while besieged and captured with only the Capitolium they cultivate the gods, which another would already have spurned as angry, and through the battle lines of the Gauls marveling at the boldness of superstition they proceed unarmed with weapons, but armed with the cult of religion, while with enemy walls captured and victory still raging they venerate the conquered deities, while from everywhere they seek foreign gods and make them their own, while they build altars sometimes even to unknown deities and to the dead. Thus while they take up the sacred rites of all nations, they also merited kingdoms. Hence the continuous course of veneration remained, which is not broken by long age, but is increased: indeed antiquity has been accustomed to grant as much sanctity to ceremonies and shrines as it has added of oldness.

lemmas.gloss: the dead, spirits of the dead

choices.why: Keeps the metaphor of ancestral teaching as a priestly office that mediates truth; 'antistes' is a cultic term, not just 'teacher'.
Uses the glossary term 'religion' and preserves the passive participle 'traditas' as 'handed down' to show ancestral transmission.
Renders 'municipes' literally as 'municipal' to convey the local, civic character of each people's gods, matching the list of peoples and their deities.
Keeps the adjective 'religiosam' with 'uirtutem' to show that Roman military courage is qualified as religious, not just 'piety in arms'.
Uses the glossary term 'superstition' and keeps the genitive construction to preserve Caecilius's ironic praise of Roman daring as superstition.

choices.english: to unknown deities and to the dead
choices.why: Renders 'numinibus' with the glossary term 'deity' and 'manibus' as 'the dead' to distinguish the two categories of altars.
rejected: unknown divine powers and spirits of the dead

pass_b_english: Since blind fortune or uncertain nature rules, then, how much more reverent and better it is to accept the teaching of our ancestors as the priest of truth, to observe the religions handed down, to worship the gods whom you were steeped by your parents in fearing before you knew them more intimately, and not to pass judgment on deities but to believe those who came before us. In a still uncultivated age, at the very birth of the world, they deserved to have gods who were either easy to serve or their kings. That is why we see throughout all empires, provinces, and towns that each people has its own rites of worship and worships its own local gods: the Eleusinians worship Ceres, the Phrygians the Mother, the Epidaurians Aesculapius, the Chaldeans Belus, the Syrians Astarte, the Taurians Diana, the Gauls Mercury, and the Romans all deities.

Thus their power and authority has seized the circuit of the whole world; thus they have extended their empire beyond the paths of the sun and the very limits of Ocean. They exercise religious virtue in arms. They fortify their city with the religions of sacred rites, with chaste virgins, with many honors and titles of priests. When they were besieged and captured except for the Capitol alone, they worshiped gods whom anyone else would already have spurned in their anger. Through the Gauls' battle lines, who marveled at the audacity of such devotion, they advance unarmed against weapons but armed with the worship of religion. While victory still raged, they venerated the conquered deities from enemy walls. They seek foreign gods everywhere and make them their own. They build altars sometimes even to unknown deities and to the shades.

Thus while they take up the sacred rites of all nations, they have also earned their kingdoms. From this the unbroken continuity of veneration has remained, which is not weakened by long age but increased: indeed antiquity has always been accustomed to grant as much sanctity to ceremonies and shrines as age has accumulated.

problems.source_quote: dum aras extruunt interdum etiam ignotis numinibus et manibus
problems.why: Latin mentions building altars to unknown deities and “hands”, not to the dead; English adds an unwarranted phrase.
problems.fix: while they build altars sometimes even to unknown deities and by hand

problems.quote: steeped in fearing from your parents
problems.source_quote: a parentibus ante inbutus es timere quam nosse familiarius
problems.why: 'inbutus es' = 'you were steeped/imbued in'; but 'from your parents' misrepresents 'a parentibus' = 'by your parents' (agency). 'Steeped in fearing from your parents' is ungrammatical English.
problems.fix: steeped by your parents in fearing before knowing them more intimately
problems.ruling: Latin ‘a parentibus … inbutus es’ = ‘imbued by your parents’; English misstates agency with ‘from’ and is ungrammatical.

problems.quote: captured with only the Capitol left
problems.why: 'citra' = 'short of' or 'except for'; 'citra solum Capitolium' = 'with only the Capitol remaining' or 'all but the Capitol captured'. 'Captured with only the Capitol left' is unclear—sounds like they were captured while the Capitol was left, but misses that the Capitol was the sole holdout.
problems.fix: captured except for the Capitol alone
problems.ruling: ‘citra solum Capitolium capti’ means ‘captured everything except the Capitol’; English implies opposite situation.

problems.quote: conquered deities of captured enemy walls
problems.why: 'hostilibus moenibus' = 'from enemy walls' or 'of the enemy walls'; 'captured enemy walls' adds 'captured' not in source for 'hostilibus'. The deities are 'conquered/vanquished', not the walls.
problems.ruling: Latin ‘hostilibus moenibus’ = ‘hostile walls’; English adds ‘captured’, altering the meaning.

problems.quote: who were either favorable or their kings
problems.source_quote: qui ... deos uel faciles habere uel reges
problems.why: Latin says gods were either easy (faciles) or kings (reges); English adds nonsensical “favorable or their kings” altering meaning.
problems.fix: who, in that rough age at the world’s birth, deserved gods that were either easy to serve or were themselves kings
problems.ruling: Latin 'faciles' means easy/approachable, not 'favorable'; 'uel reges' means 'or kings,' not 'or their kings.' Both words mistranslated.

edits.old: steeped in fearing from your parents
edits.new: steeped by your parents in fearing

edits.old: captured with only the Capitol left
edits.new: captured except for the Capitol alone

edits.old: conquered deities of captured enemy walls
who were either favorable or their kings
edits.new: who were either easy to serve or their kings

edits.old: while they build altars sometimes even to unknown deities and to the dead.
edits.new: while they build altars sometimes even to unknown deities and by hand.

fixed: addition: 'and to the dead' misreads 'manibus' (ablative of means, 'by hand'); changed to 'by hand'.
mistranslation: 'a parentibus' is agency ('by your parents'), not origin ('from'); changed to 'steeped by your parents in fearing'.
mistranslation: 'citra solum Capitolium' means 'except for the Capitol alone'; changed to 'captured except for the Capitol alone'.
mistranslation: 'hostilibus moenibus' means 'from enemy walls', not 'captured enemy walls'; changed to 'conquered deities from enemy walls'.
mistranslation: 'faciles' means 'easy to serve', not 'favorable'; changed to 'who were either easy to serve or their kings'.

problems.why: 'Manibus' here means 'to the dead' (manes), not 'by hand'. The context is altars to unknown deities and to the spirits of the dead.
problems.ruling: 'et manibus' likely ablative of 'Manes' (dead spirits), not 'by hand'; translation changes referent.

edits.old: while they build altars sometimes even to unknown deities and by hand.
edits.new: while they build altars sometimes even to unknown deities and to the dead.

fixed: Changed 'and by hand' to 'and to the dead': source 'et manibus' means 'and to the dead' (manes), not 'by hand'.

problems.why: Latin says "and hands," not "the dead"; English adds a concept not present in the source.
'Colere' here means worship/practice, not agricultural 'cultivate'; awkward with 'religiones'
problems.fix: to observe the traditions handed down

problems.why: 'Municipes' = local gods of each municipality, not 'municipal' in modern sense; 'colere' = worship
problems.ruling: municipes = local deities, colere = worship, not ‘cultivate municipal gods’

problems.quote: another would already have spurned as angry
problems.why: 'Alius' = anyone else, not 'another' specific person; 'iratos' = though angry/in their anger
problems.fix: gods which anyone else would have spurned in their anger
problems.ruling: alius = any other person, iratos = in anger; translation misstates

problems.quote: through the battle lines of Gauls marveling at the boldness of superstition
problems.source_quote: per Gallorum acies mirantium superstitionis audaciam
problems.why: Ambiguous: Gauls marvel at Roman audacity, not their own; 'superstitionis' = of their religious devotion
problems.fix: through the Gauls' battle lines, who marveled at the audacity of such devotion
problems.ruling: per Gallorum acies mirantium superstitionis audaciam mis‑rendered

problems.why: 'Manibus' = shades/spirits of the dead, not 'the dead' generally; technical religious term
problems.ruling: manibus = with their hands, not ‘to the dead’

problems.quote: grant as much sanctity to ceremonies and shrines as it has added of age
problems.source_quote: tantum sanctitatis tribuere consueuit quantum adstruxerit uetustatis
problems.why: 'Adstruxerit' = has built up/accumulated, not 'added of'; 'quantum...quantum' = as much...as
problems.fix: accustomed to grant as much sanctity to ceremonies and shrines as age has accumulated
problems.ruling: adstruxerit = built up/accumulated, not ‘added of age’

fixed: addition 'and to the dead' (source 'et manibus'): 'manibus' here means the shades/spirits of the dead, so 'to the shades' is correct.
mistranslation 'cultivate the religions handed down' (source 'religiones traditas colere'): 'colere' with 'religiones' means observe/practice, so changed to 'observe'.

mistranslation 'cultivates its own municipal gods' (source 'deos colere municipes'): 'municipes' means local gods of each town, and 'colere' means worship, so changed to 'worships its own local gods'.

mistranslation 'another would already have spurned as angry' (source 'quos alius iam spreuisset iratos'): 'alius' means anyone else, and 'iratos' means in their anger, so changed to 'anyone else would already have spurned in their anger'.

mistranslation 'through the battle lines of Gauls marveling at the boldness of superstition' (source 'per Gallorum acies mirantium superstitionis audaciam'): the Gauls marvel at the Romans' audacity, so changed to 'through the Gauls' battle lines, who marveled at the audacity of such devotion'.

mistranslation 'grant as much sanctity to ceremonies and shrines as it has added of age' (source 'tantum sanctitatis tribuere consueuit quantum adstruxerit uetustatis'): 'adstruxerit' means has built up/accumulated, so changed to 'as age has accumulated'.

problems.quote: my friend Natalis's opinion has wavered
problems.why: Caecilius is suddenly called 'Natalis' with no explanation; reader thinks a new person.
problems.fix: Add note: Natalis is an alternate name for Caecilius.

problems.why: Sentence is garbled; syntax breaks down mid-way through.

fixed: The 'Natalis' problem is not in this section; no such phrase appears in the English. No edit made.

The sentence is not garbled; it is a long periodic sentence with a series of 'while' clauses, matching the source's 'dum... dum... dum...' structure. The only issue is a missing comma after 'devotion' to set off the relative clause, which I have added.

dismissed.quote: who marveled at the audacity of such devotion
dismissed.why: 'superstitio' is glossary term for 'superstition,' not 'devotion'; Caecilius uses it positively but English must use glossary term or its sense.
dismissed.note: Caecilius speaks approvingly here, so 'superstitio' in the sense of religious scruple is fairly rendered as 'devotion'; the checker is making a mechanical glossary demand.

dismissed.why: Missing 'maiorum' (ancestors), altering who the priest represents.
dismissed.note: 'Maiorum' goes with 'disciplinam' and is translated in 'the teaching of our ancestors', so nothing is missing.

polish.changed: Broke the long garbled sentence into clear, separate statements with explicit subjects, so the reader can follow who is acting and what each pronoun refers to.
